content: Adulterants are chemical substances that are not legally or otherwise permitted to be present in other substances, such as food, beverages, fuels, or pesticides. These substances may be deliberately added to reduce manufacturing costs or for deceptive or malicious purposes. In some cases, adulterants may also be introduced accidentally or unknowingly. The process of adding adulterants is referred to as adulteration. In the context of food and beverages, examples of adulteration include the following: Seeds of the plant Coffea mogdad have been used as an adulterant in coffee. Roasted chicory roots were historically used as a coffee substitute, particularly during the Napoleonic era in France, and continue to be a moderately popular additive in cheaper coffee products. Roasted and ground peas, beans, or wheat have been used to adulterate roasted chicory. Diethylene glycol has been used by some winemakers to mimic the sweetness of high-quality sweet wines. Oleomargarine or lard has been added to butter to reduce costs. Rapeseed oil is often mixed with sunflower oil or soybean oil, with brassicasterol serving as a marker for its presence. Rye flour, cornmeal, or potato starch has been used to dilute more expensive flours, with alum sometimes added to mask the use of lower-quality flour. Apple jellies have been substituted for more expensive fruit jellies, with added colorants and even small pieces of wood to simulate strawberry seeds. Toxic artificial colorants, such as copper, zinc, or indigo-based green dyes, have been added to absinthe. Sudan I, a yellow dye, has been added to chili powder. Water has been used to dilute milk, beer, and other alcoholic beverages. Lower-quality black tea has been disguised as higher-grade tea. Starch has been added to sausages to increase bulk. Cutting agents, such as shoe polish, have been used to adulterate illicit drugs like solid cannabis. Urea and other non-protein nitrogen sources have been added to protein products to artificially inflate crude protein content measurements. Powdered beech nut husks, flavored with cinnamic aldehyde, have been marketed as powdered cinnamon. High-fructose corn syrup has been used to adulterate honey. Historically, the use of adulterants has been widespread in free-market societies with minimal legal controls on food quality and inadequate or nonexistent monitoring by authorities. In some cases, adulterants have included highly dangerous chemicals and poisons. For example, during the Victorian era in the United Kingdom, adulterants were commonly used, with some cheeses being colored with lead. Similar issues were observed in the United States until the passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act in 1906. More recently, the use of adulterants in the People's Republic of China has garnered significant public attention, particularly in relation to food safety. The first systematic investigation of adulterants was conducted in 1820 by the German chemist Frederick Accum, who identified numerous toxic metal colorants in food and beverages. However, his work provoked backlash from food suppliers, and he was discredited following a scandal involving alleged mutilation of library books at the Royal Institution. Later, in the early 1850s, the physician Arthur Hill Hassall conducted extensive studies on food adulteration, which were published in The Lancet. His findings led to the passage of the 1860 Food Adulteration Act and subsequent legislation. By the turn of the 20th century, industrialization had led to a rise in adulteration, prompting public protests. For instance, a satirical poem published in the New York Evening Post highlighted the issue of adulteration in the meatpacking industry. In the context of drug testing, adulterants may be added to urine samples to interfere with the accuracy of test results. These adulterants are often oxidative in nature, with substances such as hydrogen peroxide and bleach being used, sometimes in combination with pH-adjusting agents like vinegar or sodium bicarbonate. While drug testing laboratories can detect these adulterants, some less expensive tests may not screen for them. In 1997, ConAgra Foods pleaded guilty to federal criminal charges after one of its units illegally sprayed water on stored grain to increase its weight and value. Additionally, in the United States, authorities have identified cases of adulteration in both pet food and the human food supply. For example, melamine contamination in protein products was traced to the Xuzhou Anying Biological Technology Development Company, a company based in Xuzhou, China.
